title: Swim In Rising Water
statement: An n by n grid holds each height from 0 to n*n-1 exactly once. Water rises over time: at time t you may stand on any cell with height at most t, and you can swim between touching cells instantly. Starting at the top-left cell at time 0, find the earliest time you can stand on the bottom-right cell.

example.caption: The best path goes 0, 3, 1, 2, 4. Its highest cell is 4, so you must wait until time 4. Going through the 8 would cost more.

idea.sentence: The cost of a path is its highest cell, so run Dijkstra where a cell's cost is the larger of the cost so far and its own height.

jargon.plain: A path judged by its single worst step (here the highest cell) instead of by the sum of its steps.
Always process the cheapest unfinished item next. Only the cost rule changes: max instead of plus.
All cells you can reach at the current water level. It only grows as the level rises.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a square grid of distinct heights, e.g. [[0,3,1],[7,8,2],[6,5,4]]

vars.meaning: grid side, so there are n*n cells

compare.bruteLabel: Try each water level, flood-fill each time
compare.optimalLabel: One heap pass over the cells
compare.unit: operations (rough; heap cost is N log N for N = n*n cells)

rows.name: Each level, flood-fill
rows.note: For every time t from 0 to n*n-1, flood from the start. Each flood visits up to n*n cells.

rows.name: Binary search on time + flood-fill
rows.note: Not shown. Connectivity only improves with time, so binary search the first time the corners connect.

rows.name: Dijkstra with a heap
rows.note: Each cell enters the heap once. Each push and pop costs log of the heap size.

fast.takeaway: When a path is judged by its worst cell, the cost rule is max, and Dijkstra's greedy order still works.

stages.title: Start cell
stages.note: Push the top-left cell with its own height as its level and mark it seen.

stages.title: Pop the lowest level
stages.note: Take the waiting cell with the smallest level. That level is the lowest water that reaches it.

stages.title: Add neighbours
stages.note: Each unseen neighbour costs max(current level, its own height). Mark it seen and push it.

stages.title: Goal popped
stages.note: The first time the bottom-right cell comes out of the heap, its level is the answer.

edges.title: One cell
edges.why: Start is also the goal. The very first pop is the target and returns its level.

edges.title: Start is not the lowest
edges.why: You must stand on the start, so the answer is at least 3. Beginning the level at 0 instead of grid[0][0] would give a wrong answer.

edges.title: Goal is the lowest
edges.why: Even a very low goal cell does not help. The path still needs to cross cell 2 or 3, and 2 is cheaper.

edges.title: Longer path, lower peak
edges.why: The route down the left edge then along the bottom touches 7 as its highest. Cutting through the 8 would need 8.

gotchas.text: The path cost is max, not a sum. Push max(level, grid[nr][nc]). Adding heights would be a different, wrong problem.
Marking a cell seen when you push it is safe here. The first route to reach a cell comes from the lowest popped level, so no later route can beat it.
No built-in heap. Do not use array.sort() inside the loop. Also build seen with map, not Array(n).fill(Array(n).fill(false)), which would share one inner array across all rows.
Build the 2-D seen grid with a loop. make([][]bool, n) gives n nil rows, and indexing a nil row panics until you allocate it.
Use container/heap: heap.Push(h, x) and heap.Pop(h). Calling h.Push or h.Pop directly does not restore the heap order.

recap.key: Heap of cells by level. Pop the lowest, push neighbours with max(level, own height), stop when the goal pops.
recap.complexity: Time O(n^2 log n). Space O(n^2).
moves: Push the start with its own height
Pop the cell with the lowest level
Push each unseen neighbour at max(level, its height)
Return the level when the bottom-right cell pops
